THE FABRIC OF MEMORY
Costume, History and the Cinematic Image in The Colour of Pomegranates
10 September 2024

Iva Kontic

Instagram

In The Colour of Pomegranates (1968), Sergei Parajanov’s avant-garde film on the life of the eighteenth-century Armenian poet Sayat-Nova, costume is never mere decoration. I explore some of the key characteristics and functions of costume design in the film—the avant-garde work by the Armenian director. I try to define how the costume, conceived in the context of the film as a set of clothes, accessories, embroidery, textiles and colours, plays an essential role in constructing the film’s narrative and forming its audio-visual language and style. The costume’s specific reference to Armenian cultural heritage and history, and its particular use in the construction of the cinematic image, make it become a generator of the film’s powerful synesthetic effect and highly symbolic yet enigmatic meaning. I attempt to show that the film’s costume design isn’t just an integral part of filmmaking, the essential constituent of cinematic image and language; in The Colour of Pomegranates, it is recognised as a core agent of our reconnection to history, seen as collective memory through the cinematic experience.
When it comes to analysing the complex presence and role of costume in The Colour of Pomegranates, it is important to mention that the film was first conceived as a biopic about the eighteenth-century Armenian poet and singer Sayat-Nova, who was considered a historical figure central to the formation of Armenian cultural identity as well as to the multicultural Transcaucasian heritage. Released within the context of the USSR political and cultural reality, the film was criticised and censored by the local cinema regulatory body for not being realistic enough to qualify as a biographical film and, more broadly, as a historical film. Consequently, all the references to Sayat-Nova had to be removed from the film, including the quotations from his songs in the intertitles (except those directly integrated into the film’s scenes through the words sewn on the pieces of cloth) — making the film even more abstract and non-conventional in relation to its historical source and original film genre.¹
Citing the films of Tarkovsky and Pasolini as his main sources of inspiration, Parajanov’s filmmaking was marked by an attempt to escape the classical Soviet cinema realism, its rationalist and modernist approach, by infusing the cinematic image with surrealist moments and creating a stream-of-consciousness effect.² This surrealist, non-realistic approach to representing a historical figure, and therefore a historical moment, through mainly visual and sonic qualities of the image takes up the centre stage in The Colour of Pomegranate. The film abandons the traditional fabula of the historical genre, substituting actual historical events with poetry, ethnography, songs, performance and archaeology—and thus it “transforms a narrative retracing of history into an affective event.”³
This is where the costume design plays the essential role, since “it functions as both realism and spectacle.” Sarah Street recognises it as a part of “complex codes of verisimilitude which films use in order to convince (…) their audience, which either accord with a notion of generic verisimilitude as part of genre iconography, or with a notion of social verisimilitude (…)—costumes that convince as being realistic to appropriate situation” (in this case, appropriate to the historical circumstances outlined by the biopic).⁴ We can say that Parajanov’s ‘visual poem’ overturns this standard conception of ‘verisimilitude’ hierarchy between costume and film genre. Since the film’s historical (sur)realism brings to the same level the non-objective, highly symbolical and carefully constructed images in a collage style with the historical factuality they refer to, the costume and other ‘fashion objects’ actually become the markers in the film for establishing our relation to the real world, that is, to the objective historical reality.
Through the complex use of ethnographic costumes, traditional clothes, accessories, cultural and religious artefacts, tapestry and different textiles representative of the Armenian national heritage, the costume design in the film evokes the Armenian cultural history (identity), which is conceived as collective memory and whose experience and continuity can be only obtained through the performance of those memories embodied in language, music, dance, secular or religious customs, architecture and, of course, clothes and ‘fashion objects’ (although we can’t properly talk of ‘fashion’ in this pre-industrial context). The Colour of Pomegranate inaugurates what Patricia Pisters outlined as “the shifted interest of cinema towards history [which,] told as past past, becomes memory, (…) a past which is problematised in the present.”⁵ The same shift has been noticed by Wortel and Smelik in postmodern costume films, which seek to “produce a different experience of memory rather than a ‘correct’ representation of the past; [they] turn to performance, texture and affect for its valuable function: cinematic performance of memory allows us to experience the lived past in our present.”⁶
In this light, Parajanov’s film represents a poetic and ethnographic reconstruction of Armenian history, cultural tradition and religious identity through synesthetic experience of colour, sound, materiality (clothes, textiles, fashion and other objects, but also landscape, animals, architecture and the materiality of the analogue film itself) and movement (performative gesture).⁷

It is therefore clear how costume design here can’t be only understood as an ethnographic marker of national history and identity, the film’s realism, but as an interwoven element, the very fabric of its cinematic image, which has a strong haptic quality. This haptic sense in The Colour of Pomegranates is brought to extreme, emanating from the abundance of textiles and fabrics that constitute the costumes and other fashion objects. The materiality of the dresses, tapestries, rugs and clothes, wool, lace, jewellery, hats and other accessories is reflected to that one of the multitude of film props and symbolic objects (sheep, roosters, pomegranates, bread, grapes, books, dishes, armature, church relics, hay, earth, feathers)—and together they integrate into the materiality of the architectural sites, another important element through which the film’s meaning and esthetic value is structured.⁸
The lack of depth field in the film’s images brings all the given materialities to one single plane, which perfectly corresponds to the graininess of analogue film. Together they give the surface of the cinematic image a tactile quality, as if we were not looking at the screen but into a textile surface. As if the film itself were one of those tapestries and embroideries displayed in its tableaux-vivant-like scenes; or as if it were a Persian miniature painting referenced in the filmic construction of those ‘living pictures’, which are heavily reminiscent of early cinema (or better, prehistoric cinema). The film becomes part of that very heritage which is representative of the local cultural identity—thus evoking the materiality of collective memory.
The synesthetic concept of the poetic cinema of Parajanov, closely linked to its costume design and essential to the film’s conception of history, expands further into the sphere of the olfactory, even the gustatory, through the interaction with them (the vapor from the wool-dyeing, the red liquid (blood) in the sacrifice of lambs, the touching and kissing of earth mixed with bread, etc.). Historical reality is transformed into a synesthetic spectacle, bringing the costume’s double role in cinema—as realism and spectacle—to the equation.
The rich, complex, meticulously constructed symbology and meaning of each fashion and non-fashion object (e.g., the colours of the dyed wools indicate the Armenian flag), together with their performative interaction with the characters and their bodies, give us potential access to the film’s historical reality and its interpretation. This access seems to depend on a close knowledge of the local cultural heritage and history; yet it always leaves us ‘at the entrance’, always remaining within the realm of mystery and ambiguity. Just like the costumes, conceived by Parajanov himself⁹—therefore not authentic artefacts but sartorial pieces—this ‘poetic biopic’ short-circuits the opposing trends of modern cinema, which Bazin identified as either placing faith in the image or trusting in reality.¹⁰
By the same token, the performative aspect of the film—especially the relationship between the performing bodies and the clothes — becomes fundamental to its oscillation between different cinematographic approaches and styles, between meaning and ambiguity, reality and spectacle, cinematic narration and history. The static, pictorial reality of The Colour of Pomegranates is animated exclusively by characters’ performances, which seem shaped by the form and materiality of the garments and cloth. The abundance of fabrics, textures and colours of the latter seems to correspond to the reduction and minimalism of the former.
Similarly, the costume both supports and provokes the sexual ambiguity created by the same actress performing both Sayat-Nova and his wife (as well as several other characters). Cross-dressing and the alteration of objects that function as ‘gender-indicators’ (e.g. the shell and knitting needles) create a Deleuzian ‘mirror-image’, in which the real and the imaginary, the present and the past ‘coalesce’, distinct yet indiscernible in a state of continuous reversibility.¹¹ Together with the frequent acts of dressing, undressing, knitting, dancing with tapestry on the sound of popular Sayat-Nova music, they generate a particular performance of collective memory.
The national history and cultural identity are not simply represented and preserved but are put in the continuous “process of ‘becoming’, (…) a dynamic practice of metamorphosis”¹² where memory (or, “invention of people”¹³) continually moves between written word, artefacts, clothes, music, myths and customs, architectural ruins, geographic and political landscape, technology—between past, present and future.

Notes

¹  As part of the modifications, the director was forced to change the film’s original title Sayat-Nova to The Colour of Pomegranates. It was only recently (2014) that the film was restored according to Parajanov’s original version and re-released: “The Color of Pomegranates, a Film by Sergei Parajanov,” Parajanov-Vartanov Institute, December 15, 2023, parajanov.com/thecolorofpomegranates.

²  Dimitar Kutmanov, “The Cinema of Sergei Parajanov,” Dimitar Kutmanov (portfolio), accessed August 31, 2024, kutmanov.weebly.com.

³  Elise Wortel and Annike Smelik, “Textures of Time: A Becoming Memory of History in Costume Film,” in Performing Memory in Art and Popular Culture, ed. Liedeke Plate and Anneke Smelik (Routledge, 2013), 185–200.
⁴  Sarah Street, Costume and Cinema: Dress Codes in Popular Film (Wallflower, 2002), 7.
⁵  Patricia Pisters, “The Open Archive: Cinema and World-Memory,” in The Neuro-Image: A Deleuzian Film-Philosophy of Digital Screen Culture (Stanford University Press, 2012), 225.

⁶  Elise Wortel and Annike Smelik, “Textures of Time,” 185–200.
⁷ Ibid.
⁸ The film was shot at several historic locations in Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan which were important in the life of Sayat-Nova but also for the history of the Armenian people — e.g. Haghpat Monastery, where the poet-singer had lived as a monk in his later years: Curtis Tsui, “10 Things I Learned: The Color of Pomegranates,” The Criterion Collection, May 9, 2018, criterion.com/current/posts/5639.

PHROOM

THE FABRIC OF MEMORY
Costume, History and the Cinematic Image in The Colour of Pomegranates
10 September 2024

Iva Kontic

Instagram

In El color de las granadas (1968), la película vanguardista de Sergei Parajanov sobre la vida del poeta armenio del siglo XVIII Sayat-Nova, el traje nunca es una mera decoración. Exploro algunas de las características y funciones clave del diseño de vestuario en la película: el trabajo vanguardista del director armenio. Trato de definir cómo el disfraz, concebido en el contexto de la película como un conjunto de ropa, accesorios, colores de referencia, colores textiles y El color de las granadas, es reconocido como un agente fundamental de nuestra reconexión a la historia, vista como memoria colectiva a través de la experiencia cinematográfica.
Cuando se trata de analizar la compleja presencia y el papel del traje en El color de las granadas, es importante mencionar que la película fue concebida por primera vez como biopic sobre el poeta y cantante armenio del siglo XVIII Sayat-Nova, que fue considerado una figura histórica central en la formación de la identidad cultural armenia, así como en el patrimonio multicultural transcaucasiano. Liberado en el contexto de la realidad política y cultural de la URSS, la película fue criticada y censurada por el cuerpo regulador del cine local por no ser lo suficientemente realista como para calificar como un género de película de película de película de película de película de película
Citando las películas de Tarkovsky y Pasolini como sus principales fuentes de inspiración, la filmación de Parajanov fue marcada por un intento de escapar del realismo clásico del cine soviético, su enfoque racionalista y modernista, infundiendo la imagen cinematográfica con momentos surrealistas y creando un efecto de corriente de conciencia.2 Este enfoque surrealista y no realista para representar una figura histórica, y por lo tanto un momento histórico, hasta la imagen visual El color de la granada. La película abandona la tradicional fabula del género histórico, sustituyendo hechos históricos reales con poesía, etnografía, canciones, performance y arqueología, y por lo tanto “transforma una retracción narrativa de la historia en un evento afectivo.”3
Es aquí donde el diseño de vestuario juega el papel esencial, ya que “actua como realismo y espectáculo”. Sarah Street lo reconoce como parte de “códigos complejos de verisimilitud que usan las películas para convencer (...) a su público, que coinciden con una noción de verisimilitud genérica como parte de la iconografía del género, o con una noción de verisimilitud social (...)
A través del complejo uso de trajes etnográficos, ropas tradicionales, accesorios, artefactos culturales y religiosos, tapiz y diferentes textiles representativos del patrimonio nacional armenio, el diseño de trajes en la película evoca la historia cultural armenia (identidad), que se concibe como memoria colectiva y cuya experiencia y continuidad sólo se puede obtener a través de la interpretación de esos recuerdos encarnados en lenguaje, música, danza, costumbres seculares o religiosas, arquitectura y, por supuesto, ropa y 'conversidad propiamente El color de la granada inaugura lo que Patricia Pisters delineó como “el interés cambiante del cine hacia la historia [que,] dicho como pasado, se convierte en memoria, (...) un pasado que se encuentra problemático en el presente.”5 El mismo cambio ha sido notado por Wortel y Smelik en películas de vestuario postmodernas, que buscan “producir una experiencia diferente de memoria en lugar de una representación ‘correcta’ del pasado; [ellos] se convierten en performance, textura y afectuada del cine
En este sentido, la película de Parajanov representa una reconstrucción poética y etnográfica de la historia armenia, la tradición cultural y la identidad religiosa a través de la experiencia sintética del color, el sonido, la materialidad (clothes, textiles, moda y otros objetos, pero también paisaje, animales, arquitectura y la materialidad de la película analógica en sí) y movimiento (sello performativo)7.

Por lo tanto, está claro cómo el diseño de vestuario no sólo puede entenderse como un marcador etnográfico de la historia e identidad nacional, el realismo de la película, sino como un elemento entrelazado, el tejido mismo de su imagen cinematográfica, que tiene una fuerte calidad hepática. El color de las granadas es llevado a extremo, emanando de la abundancia de textiles y telas que constituyen los trajes y otros objetos de moda. La materialidad de los vestidos, tapices, alfombras y ropa, lana, encaje, joyería, sombreros y otros accesorios se refleja en que una de las multitudes de propulsores de película y objetos simbólicos (cama, gallos, granadas, pan, uvas, libros, plumas, plumas, armaduras, objetos de la iglesia)
La falta de campo de profundidad en las imágenes de la película trae todas las materialidades dadas a un solo plano, que corresponde perfectamente a la granosidad de la película analógica. Juntos dan a la superficie de la imagen cinematográfica una calidad táctil, como si no estuvieramos mirando a la pantalla sino a una superficie textil. Como si la película en sí fuera una de esas tapices y bordados exhibidos en sus escenas de referencias de tableaux; o como si
El concepto sinestético del cine poético de Parajanov, estrechamente ligado a su diseño de vestuario y esencial a la concepción de la historia de la película, se expande aún más en la esfera de la olfativa, incluso la gustatoria, a través de la interacción con ellos (el vapor de la teñida de la lana, el líquido rojo (sangre) en el sacrificio de los corderos, el toque y el beso de la tierra mezclado con el pan, etc.
La rica, compleja, meticulosa simbología y significado de cada objeto de moda y de no moda (por ejemplo, los colores de las lanas teñidas indican la bandera armenia), junto con su interacción performativa con los personajes y sus cuerpos, nos dan acceso potencial a la realidad histórica de la película y su interpretación.Este acceso parece depender de un conocimiento cercano del patrimonio cultural local y la historia; sin embargo siempre nos deja ‘en el misterio
De la misma manera, el aspecto performativo de la película —especialmente la relación entre los cuerpos escénicos y la ropa— se convierte en fundamental para su oscilación entre diferentes enfoques cinematográficos y estilos, entre significado y ambigüedad, realidad y espectáculo, narración cinematográfica e historia. El color de las granadas se anima exclusivamente por las actuaciones de los personajes, que parecen conformadas por la forma y la materialidad de las prendas y telas. La abundancia de telas, texturas y colores de este último parece corresponder a la reducción y el minimalismo de la primera.
Del mismo modo, el traje soporta y provoca la ambigüedad sexual creada por la misma actriz que interpreta a Sayat-Nova y a su esposa (así como a varios otros personajes). El cruce y la alteración de objetos que funcionan como ‘indicadores de género’ (por ejemplo, la cáscara y agujas de punto) crean un ‘image de espejo’ deleuziano, en el que el estado real e imaginario repite
La historia nacional y la identidad cultural no son simplemente representadas y preservadas, sino que se ponen en el continuo “proceso de ‘venir’, (...) una práctica dinámica de la metamorfosis”12 donde la memoria (o, “invención de personas”13) se mueve continuamente entre la palabra escrita, los artefactos, la ropa, la música, los mitos y las costumbres, las ruinas arquitectónicas, el paisaje geográfico y político, la tecnología—entre pasado, presente y futuro.

Notas

¹ Como parte de las modificaciones, el director se vio obligado a cambiar el título original de la película Sayat-Nova al color de los granados. Recientemente (2014) la película fue restaurada según la versión original de Parajanov y reeditada: “El color de los granados, una película de Sergei Parajanov”, Instituto Parajanov-Vartanov, 15 de diciembre de 2023, parajatheponov.

2 Dimitar Kutmanov, “El Cine de Sergei Parajanov”, Dimitar Kutmanov (portfolio), accedido el 31 de agosto de 2024, kutmanov.weebly.com.

³ Elise Wortel y Annike Smelik, “Texturas del tiempo: Una memoria de la historia en el cine de vestuario”, en la memoria de la cultura popular y el arte, ed. Liedeke Plate y Anneke Smelik (Routledge, 2013), 185–200.
⁴ Sarah Street, Disfraz y Cine: Códigos de Vestido en Película Popular (Wallflower, 2002), 7.
5 Patricia Pisters, “El Archivo Abierto: Cine y World-Memory”, en The Neuro-Image: A Deleuzian Film-Philosophy of Digital Screen Culture (Stanford University Press, 2012), 225.

6 Elise Wortel y Annike Smelik, “Texturas del tiempo”, 185–200.
7 Ibíd.
8 La película fue filmada en varios lugares históricos en Armenia, Georgia y Azerbaiyán, que eran importantes en la vida de Sayat-Nova, pero también en la historia del pueblo armenio —por ejemplo, Monasterio Haghpat, donde el poeta-singer había vivido como monje en sus años posteriores: Curtis Tsui, “10 cosas que aprendí: el color de los granados”, The Criterion Collection, 9 de mayo de 2018, criteriocomcurrent.
9 Ibíd.
10 André Bazin, ¿Qué es el cine? (Universidad de California Press, 1967), 24.

NOTES ON CINEMA
Medium, Politics, Experience
8 November 2025

Iva Kontic

Instagram

Three short reflections on what cinema is and does.

Rethinking Cinema as Medium: A Deleuzian Approach

In his theorisation of cinema as a medium, Gilles Deleuze deals with cinema at the level of image—as it appears to us—rather than analysing the cinematic medium as a language (a system of signs) or as an apparatus (its technology and the technical devices it employs from its conception to its display). He states: “cinema seems to us a composition of images and signs (a pre-verbal intelligible content) (…) which change with historical circumstances” (Deleuze, 1986, p.ix). What remains constant is the cinematic concept, which is represented by various types of images and signs that “correspond to each type” of images (p.ix). The cinematic concept is thus central for understanding the specificity of cinema as a generator of concepts—of “images of thoughts” (p.xi)—much as philosophy is. Deleuze places cinema’s ‘concept production’ in accordance with its own specific elements alongside—if not above—cinema’s conception as an art form. The given line of thought does not, however, imply distancing cinema from other forms of art production. Rather, it fits into a general trend within the visual arts, which moves away from understanding art as merely ‘retinal’, as an aesthetic form, as a faculty of what Bazin (1958) calls ‘pseudo-realism’ (p.6), toward embracing a notion of art that privileges ideas, the process of concept-making—a trend that started at the beginning of the 20th century (just as cinema was establishing itself as an artistic medium) and which continues today.
To identify the specificity of the cinematic concept, it is first necessary to pinpoint the essential features of the cinematic image. For Deleuze, the cinematic image is ‘automatic’, a product of mechanical devices (camera, projector), and is presented to the spectator as either movement-image or time-image (post-WWII cinema). These are two distinct regimes of the cinematic image, each representing time differently. Nevertheless, time remains central to both image regimes—and, consequently, to the cinematic concept itself—whether represented indirectly through movement (through the movement-images themselves or their distribution via montage) or written directly into the time-image. I will focus on the movement-image as the essence of the cinematic medium: what makes it novel in relation to the photographic image (from which it derives) and which differentiates it from human perception (whose desire for imitation brought cinema into being).
The movement-image is not a sum of instances, of immobile sections that reconstruct movement by adding time; it is already movement, characterised by constant change and a concrete duration. For Deleuze, this marks a break with human perception. While the reconstruction of movement occurs in the human mind/eye (a correction that creates an illusion of movement), that very illusion is already resolved within the cinematic apparatus itself, which presents photograms (frames) in a temporal flow. What the spectator sees, therefore, are ‘real’ movement-images, not a reconstruction of real movement. Cinema’s status as a non-human perception became more evident once it developed as an art form—in modernist terms, when it embraced its specificity as a medium and freed itself from imitation of natural perception—through “montage, the mobile camera and the emancipation of the viewpoint” (p.3). Moreover, cinema reproduces movement composed not of ‘poses’, of privileged instants (a transcendental synthesis of an entire movement) but of ‘any-instant-whatevers’ (immanent material elements that analyse a movement), always equidistant from one another so as to give an impression of continuity (p.4–5). Cinema, in other words, can’t be understood as photographs placed in sequence. The cinematic sections, or instants, are in fact ‘banalities’ which, through accumulation, produce ‘singularities’, generating “the qualitative leap” (p.6). Such features clearly mark a radical break from traditional fine art practices interested in ideal, timeless forms—which stands in sharp contrast to cinema’s unprivileged ‘any-instant-whatevers’. From today’s vantage point, however, the given aspect is no longer a specificity unique to cinema—no longer a point of differentiation between cinema, as ‘industrial art’, and the rest of the visual arts—given how art itself has evolved over the course of the 20th century. Performance art, video art, new media art are all likewise non-transcendental, while the latter two could be equally considered ‘industrial’ and mass-mediatic. Although cinema gave rise to a new art form, it no longer holds a ‘special position’ among the visual arts, at least not at the level of the cinematic image.¹
One reason Deleuze’s conceptualisation of cinema has withstood the ‘tests of time’ is that he grants the cinematic image a space of emancipation from the constraints of ‘reality’ by distinguishing cinematic perception from human perception. In this way, the essence of the moving-image remains unchanged and applicable to analog cinema and to the contemporary culture of the digital image. The objectivity of the cinematic image in relation to the reality it traces—which is central to Bazin’s (1958) belief in cinema’s ‘realism’ (p.3–12) and undermined by the evolution of image-production technologies—is bypassed by placing the ‘responsibility’ for illusion (for the falsification of reality) on the cinematic apparatus itself (camera/projector), thereby taking it away from the cinematic image and the spectator. The spectator’s belief in the cinematic image thus becomes, in a sense, beside the point—whether they are viewing a continuous or ‘discrete image’ (Stiegler, 1995, p.147–163)—without essentially altering the way that cinema produces autonomous forms of art/thought through cinematic images and corresponding signs.

Cinema and Politics: Missing People, the Oppositional Gaze, and The Headless Woman

I will briefly examine the relationship between cinema and politics through the lens of Gilles Deleuze’s conceptualisation of ‘modern political cinema’ and bell hooks’ notion of ‘oppositional gaze’. These two theoretical approaches address distinct, yet neither oppositional nor mutually exclusive, categories of politics: the former broadly focused on the politics of minorities, the latter situated within the intersectional politics of race and gender. Both are concerned with identity politics in cinema, and both tackle the issues of diversity and inclusion within the framework of post-colonial thought. To show how these concepts can interact and complement one another, I want to put them into play by analysing Lucrecia Martel’s La mujer sin cabeza (“The Headless Woman”, 2008), arguing that this psychological thriller can be classified as political cinema—in which the genre itself operates in the service of social engagement.
At the core of Deleuze’s concept of ‘modern political cinema’ are two big absences that cinema announces and makes visible.² In the new political cinema, the people are missing (Deleuze, 1989, p.216)—they are excluded from the dominant narratives belonging to others, the colonisers, but are also colonised by their own impersonalised myths—which makes the colonisation and the identity fragmentation work from the outside and from the inside (Deleuze calls this the faculty of ‘double becoming’) (p.221). The second lack is that of the boundary between the spheres of the political and the private, which makes it impossible for the people—whose memories are neither psychological nor collective—to become conscious through the process of evolution or revolution. Deleuze, thus, defines modern political cinema as the cinema of the Third World, of the minorities, and of their ‘impossibility of living’ (p.219)—where the failure of identity fusion is acknowledged and the only thing left is a constant exchange between “a fragmented world and (…) a fragmented I” (p.221).
In these terms, La mujer sin cabeza can be viewed as the modern political cinema par excellence. Nothing is made more evident during the 87 minutes of the film than the absence of the people, that is, of the poor population (often of Indigenous origin or mestizo) within the Argentinian society divided by class and ethnicity. Except in rare moments, their presence and their reality are purposely cut, blurred, ignored and marginalised by the camera. As they appear in the role of domestic help, gardeners, caretakers and other types of assistance to the wealthy bourgeoisie, their faces are left undefined and without a portrait (identity on the iconographic level)—often seen from the inside of the car window. Their existence on screen is reduced to merely providing service to the main protagonist, Veronica, and her well-off family.³ Deleuze’s concept of ‘missing people’ expands as well to the identity crisis of the protagonist herself, metaphorically indicated in the film’s title—“the woman with the missing head”. After Veronica’s car hits a dog and (most probably) an Indigenous boy from the poor local community, her self-centred (or better, hair-centred) consciousness becomes fractured by shock, guilt and remorse, but also by her realisation of her privileged position, her belonging to the white, wealthy elite within the segregated society—which gives her the possibility of ‘conscious reversal’ (p.219), in this case, of ignoring and denial. It seems impossible for her to live, at least not as before.⁴
The same motives of lack, impossibility, identity crisis and double colonisation which Martel’s film brings up can be equally read through a feminist prism and, specifically, through bell hooks’ concept of ‘oppositional gaze’. Hooks develops this notion as an acquired strategy of resistance to the dominating, oppressive white gaze which, by means of mass media, television and mainstream cinema, controls and negates the representation of black identity. Hooks confirms Stuart Hall’s idea of “white representation of blackness as totalising” (as cited in hooks, 1996, p.254)—the ‘white presence’ being a power that is external and internal to black people.⁵ The oppositional gaze is a critical, interrogating and politicised way of looking, one that grants agency to black spectatorship in changing the reality. She particularly addresses the vulnerable position of black female spectators whose representation on the big screen has been missing or marginalised, often reduced to a simplistic presence in service of white characters or as an object of the black male gaze. Since this oppression concerns two aspects of their identity—gender and race—hooks criticises white feminist film theorists for failing to actively engage with the issue of black female spectatorship and its (under)representation in cinema.
Although hooks deals with discrimination and underrepresentation of African-American women in mainstream cinema, an analogous issue can be discussed concerning the race-gender-class oppression and colonisation of female identity—which La mujer sin cabeza addresses in its social commentary. Here again, Martel’s film works on two levels. First, it emphasises the total negation of an alternative concept of female beauty (which, in the film, is equated with female identity), that is, of the non-white, non-European/Caucasian woman. The faceless, peripheral Indigenous women—like the rest of the ‘missing people’—are reduced to mere function, service, movie extras. The only non-white female figure offered to the spectator is the school friend of Veronica’s young cousin. However, her feminine identity exists only as an extension of the hidden lesbian inclinations of the privileged rich girl. This is underlined by her merging back into the blurred community of the poor local neighbourhood (the background) after she gets out of Veronica’s car.
Secondly, Martel’s film displays a more subtle, internal process of colonisation by the dominant model of feminine identity proposed by classic Hollywood—the elegant, well-mannered blond girl with a bourgeois pedigree—to which the main protagonist is subjected. The central motif in the film—Veronica’s blond hair—is contemporarily a symbol of her bourgeois femininity and of her colonised, oppressed feminine identity. She tries to fight this by changing her hair colour, but, as the film seems to suggest, the radical change in the relations of dominating discourses and oppressed minorities isn’t only a question of appearance, of the visual. It requires a more profound shift in social structures and in the distribution of power and wealth—a change that starts from the critical, oppositional gaze of each of us as spectators and social agents (one which Martel herself embraces and awakens in the spectators through her film).

Cinema as Experience: The Eye and the Body

In her seminal essay The Tactile Eye: Touch and the Cinematic Experience, Jennifer M. Barker introduces the notion of “tactile eye” to theorise film spectatorship by grounding it in the idea of a materially embodied cinematic experience, where perception and expression happen through ‘tactility’ (2009, p.1–22). She defines ‘tactility’ as “a relationship with the [cinematic] world that is at once a mutual and intimate relation of contact”, which involves the entire body, not only its surface (p.3). This concept presupposes the existence of a film’s body that is separate from the reality shown on the film screen and from the spectators themselves, but also from the film director, the cinematographer, or other participants in the film’s production. According to Barker, the film itself is capable of perceiving the reality it films and sharing its experience, which it projects, in a manner similar to the spectator. Therefore, the cinematic experience can be interpreted as a reciprocal and reversible relationship between the embodied spectator and the embodied film. The interaction between their consciousnesses, their relationships to space and time, their being in the world⁶ (within their physical, historical, socio-political and cultural contexts) forms the foundation of their relationship, through which the emotions and the meaning of the film are generated.
To illustrate Barker’s idea of tactile cinematic perception and the film’s body, I turn once more to La mujer sin cabeza, and try to look at the film from a different angle than previously. One notices, right from the start of the film—from the opening scenes, which set up both the film’s plot and its overall aesthetic approach—the alternating disconnections and interrelations between the camerawork, the sound and the actors/characters, as well as between the filmed reality and the cinematic image. At times, we see certain characters on screen but hear voices off-screen (as in the scene depicting the main protagonist and other women with their children talking around their cars). At times, the sound finds unity with the image, only to disconnect again. This unity is often displayed through reflections—direct contact with the film’s reality being denied to the spectator by the presence of car windows and other types of windows and mirrors, which announce their analogy with the film screen itself. Their presence is also rendered highly material through the emphasis placed on their textural quality (as with the child’s handprints or raindrops on the car window).
A similarly strongly tactile sensation is produced, and put in relation to the spectator’s sensory perception, through the constant touching, caressing and wetting of Veronica’s hair. Throughout the film, the camera rarely offers the opportunity to coherently and immersively follow the depicted reality or the dialogues. One seems constantly pulled in and out of the scenes through the use of particular angles, fragmented and asymmetric shots, blurred surroundings, and the overlapping of sounds from different sources, followed by their sudden silencing. The camera’s universe appears to revolve around the portrait of Veronica, yet this identification with her subjectivity is renounced through the film’s bodily presence at several crucial moments—as when the camera ceases to follow her actions and positioning in space (for instance, in the scene of the car accident, she gets out of the car, but the camera remains fixed, gazing at the door window from the car’s interior, leaving the spectator without a point of reference).
It is difficult not to see all the above-mentioned aspects as a series of strategic tools employed to stimulate a particular kind of emotion in the spectators and to guide their interpretation of the film’s meaning. Consequently, it is hard to understand how it is possible to distinguish the film’s body, which relates to the spectator’s body, from the film’s production as a whole (understood here as the film director and all those involved in the filmmaking, their decisions, work and the technology they employed), as Barker seems to suggest in her essay; nor why she finds it necessary to do so.
In effect, by implying an embodied exchange between the film and the viewer, rather than a one-way process of absorption (of being ‘lost in the film’), Barker’s theorisation of the cinematic experience can be particularly useful when it comes to forming a critical spectatorship in relation to the filmic reality and to the film itself as a cultural and artistic product—especially in the case of films that represent true-to-life characters and locations and address socio-politically sensitive issues (as La mujer sin cabeza does, in terms of class and ethnic divisions in Argentinian society). Declaring the film’s body and foregrounding the notion of tactile cinematic perception places emphasis on the process of intellectual, emotional and physical negotiation—by both the spectator and the film (that is, by its director and other participants in the filmmaking)—with the cinematic reality and the social reality that the film displays and addresses.

Notes
¹ Nor could it have been accepted as ‘art’ without the parallel radical changes in the conception of art in general, brought about by modernity.
² It is impossible to include all the aspects of the two theoretical approaches, and I will focus particularly on those aspects which are important to the analysis of the selected film.
³ The only two potential ‘subjects’, the brother of the killed boy and the school friend of Veronica’s young cousin, are individualised only insofar as they serve Veronica’s guilty conscience and her cousin’s sexual interests.
⁴Or should we say almost impossible — the director leaves this question open.
⁵ In these words, one can also recognise Deleuze’s conception of ‘double becoming’.
⁶ Here, Barker refers to the existential phenomenology of Maurice Merleau-Ponty (p.17–19).

—Bazin, André (1958/1967). “Ontology of the Photographic Image.” In What is Cinema? Vol. 1 (pp. 3–12). Berkeley–Los Angeles: University of California Press.

NOTES ON CINEMA
Medium, Politics, Experience
8 de noviembre de 2025

Iva Kontic

Instagram

Tres breves reflexiones sobre lo que es y hace el cine.

Repensar el cine como medio: un enfoque deleuziano

En su teorización del cine como medio, Gilles Deleuze se ocupa del cine a nivel de la imagen, como nos parece, en lugar de analizar el medio cinematográfico como un lenguaje (un sistema de signos) o como un aparato (la tecnología y los dispositivos técnicos que emplea desde su concepción hasta su visualización).
Para identificar la especificidad del concepto cinematográfico, primero es necesario definir las características esenciales de la imagen cinematográfica. Para Deleuze, la imagen cinematográfica es "automática", un producto de dispositivos mecánicos (camera, proyector), y se presenta al espectador como imagen de movimiento o tiempo-imagen ( cine post-WII). Estos son dos regímenes distintos de la imagen cinematográfica, cada uno representando el tiempo de manera diferente.
El movimiento-image no es una suma de instancias, de secciones inmóviles que reconstruyen el movimiento añadiendo el tiempo; ya es movimiento, caracterizado por un cambio constante y una duración concreta. Para Deleuze, esto marca una ruptura con la percepción humana.
Una razón por la cual la conceptualización del cine de Deleuze se ha resistido a las ‘pruebas del tiempo’ es que otorga a la imagen cinematográfica un espacio de emancipación de las limitaciones de la ‘realidad’ al distinguir la percepción cinematográfica de la percepción humana. De esta manera, la esencia de la imagen móvil sigue siendo invariable y aplicable al cine analógico y a la cultura contemporánea de la imagen digital.

Cine y política: personas desaparecidas, la lucha oposicional y la mujer sin cabeza

Examinaré brevemente la relación entre el cine y la política a través de la lente de Gilles Deleuze conceptualización de la noción de ‘ cinematografía política moderna’ y ganchos de campana’ de ‘visión oposicional’. Estos dos enfoques teóricos abordan distintas, sin embargo, no opositoras ni mutuamente excluyentes, categorías de política: la primera se centra ampliamente en la política de las minorías, la segunda se sitúa dentro de la política interseccional de la raza y el género. La mujer sin cabeza (“La mujer sin cabeza”, 2008), argumentando que este thriller psicológico puede ser clasificado como cine político, en el que el género mismo opera al servicio del compromiso social.
En el centro del concepto de Deleuze de ‘ cine político moderno’ hay dos grandes ausencias que el cine anuncia y hace visible.2 En el nuevo cine político, la gente se está perdiendo (Deleuze, 1989, p.216) – están excluidos de las narraciones dominantes de otros, los colonizadores, pero también son colonizados por sus propios mitos impersonalizados – que hace que la colonización y la fragmentación de identidad funcionen desde el exterior y desde el interior (Deleuze no llama así a esta facultad de "doble convertirse") (p.221).
En estos términos, La mujer sin cabeza se puede ver como el cine político moderno par excelencia. Nada se hace más evidente durante los 87 minutos de la película que la ausencia del pueblo, es decir, de la población pobre (a menudo de origen indígena o mestizo) dentro de la sociedad argentina dividida por clase y etnia. Excepto en momentos raros, su presencia y su realidad se cortan, difuminan, ignoran y marginan por la cámara.
Los mismos motivos de la falta, imposibilidad, crisis de identidad y doble colonización que la película de Martel plantea pueden leerse por igual a través de un prisma feminista y, específicamente, a través del concepto de “opuesta mirada” de los ganchos masculinos. Los ganchos desarrollan esta noción feminista como estrategia adquirida de resistencia a la mirada blanca dominante, opresiva que, por medios de comunicación masivos, televisión y cine corriente, controla
Aunque los ganchos se ocupan de la discriminación y la subrepresentación de las mujeres afroamericanas en el cine general, se puede discutir una cuestión análoga en relación con la opresión de la raza y la colonización de la identidad femenina, que La mujer sin cabeza La película de Martel funciona en dos niveles. En primer lugar, enfatiza la negación total de un concepto alternativo de belleza femenina (que, en la película, se equipara con la identidad femenina), es decir, de la mujer no blanca, no europea/caucasiana. Las mujeres indígenas sin rostro, como el resto de la ‘personas desaparecidas’, se reducen a la mera función de la película femenina, servicio privilegiado
En segundo lugar, la película de Martel muestra un proceso interno más sutil de colonización por el modelo dominante de identidad femenina propuesto por el clásico Hollywood, la elegante y bien oprimida chica rubia con un pedigrí burgués, a la que se somete el protagonista principal.El motivo central de la película —el pelo rubio de Veronica— es contemporalmente un símbolo de su feminidad burguesa y de su mirada radical

Cine como experiencia: El ojo y el cuerpo

En su ensayo seminal El ojo táctil: el tacto y la experiencia cinematográficaPor lo tanto, Jennifer M. Barker introduce la noción de “ojo retroactivo” a la espectadora de la película al basarla en la idea de una experiencia cinematográfica materialmente encarnada, donde la percepción y la expresión suceden a través de la “tactilidad” (2009, p.1–22).
Para ilustrar la idea de Barker de la percepción cinematográfica táctil y el cuerpo de la película, me vuelvo una vez más para La mujer sin cabeza, y tratar de mirar la textura desde un ángulo diferente al anterior. Una nota, desde el comienzo de la película, desde las escenas de apertura, que establecen tanto la trama de la película como su enfoque estético general, las desconexiones alternadas e interrelaciones entre la cámara, el sonido y los actores/caractores, así como entre la realidad filmada y la imagen cinematográfica.
Se produce una sensación tátil muy fuerte y se relaciona con la percepción sensorial del espectador, a través del toque constante, el cuidado y el tejado del pelo de Verónica. A lo largo de la película, la cámara raramente ofrece la oportunidad de seguir de forma coherente e inmersiva la realidad representada o los diálogos. Uno parece constantemente arrastrado y fuera de las escenas a través del uso de ángulos particulares, fragmentados y asimétricos
Es difícil no ver todos los aspectos mencionados anteriormente como una serie de herramientas estratégicas empleadas para estimular un tipo particular de emoción en los espectadores y para guiar su interpretación del significado de la película. Por consiguiente, es difícil entender cómo es posible distinguir el cuerpo de la película, que se refiere al cuerpo del espectador, de la producción en su conjunto (es decir, director de cine y todo lo que se dedica a la toma de la tecnología, así que ella lo hace necesario
En efecto, al implicar un intercambio encarnado entre la película y el espectador, en lugar de un proceso de absorción unilateral (de ser ‘perdido en la película’), la teorización de la experiencia cinematográfica de Barker puede ser particularmente útil cuando se trata de formar una mirada crítica en relación a la realidad cinematográfica y a la propia película como producto cultural y artístico, especialmente en el caso de películas que representan personajes sensibles y sensibles a la vida La mujer sin cabeza lo hace, en términos de divisiones de clase y etnia en la sociedad argentina). Declarar el cuerpo del filme y poner en primer plano la noción de percepción cinematográfica táctil pone énfasis en el proceso de negociación intelectual, emocional y física, tanto por el espectador como por la película (es decir, por su director y otros participantes en la filmación) —con la realidad cinematográfica y la realidad social que la película muestra y aborda.

Notas
1 Tampoco pudo haber sido aceptado como «arte» sin los cambios radicales paralelos en la concepción del arte en general, provocados por la modernidad.
2 Es imposible incluir todos los aspectos de los dos enfoques teóricos, y me centraré especialmente en los aspectos que son importantes para el análisis de la película seleccionada.
3 Los únicos dos posibles ‘sujetos’, el hermano del niño muerto y el amigo de la escuela del primo joven de Verónica, están individualizados sólo en la medida en que sirven a la conciencia culpable de Verónica y a los intereses sexuales de su primo.
4O deberíamos decir casi imposibles; el director deja esta pregunta abierta.
5 En estas palabras, también se puede reconocer la concepción de Deleuze de «doble convertirse».
6 Aquí, Barker se refiere a la fenomenología existencial de Maurice Merleau-Ponty (p.17-19).

Referencias
—Barker, Jennifer M. (2009). “Introducción”. El ojo táctil: el tacto y la experiencia cinematográfica (pp.1–22). Berkeley-Los Angeles: University of California Press.
—Bazin, André (1958/1967). “Ontología de la imagen fotográfica”. ¿Qué es Cinema? Vol. 1 (pág. 3–12). Berkeley-Los Angeles: University of California Press.
—Deleuze, Gilles (1989). “Cinema, Cuerpo y Cerebro, Pensamiento”. Cine II: La imagen del tiempo (pp. 215–224). Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.
—Deleuze, Gilles (1986). “Tesis del movimiento”. Cine I: La imagen del movimiento (pp. ix–11). Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.
-hooks, bell (1996). “El Gaze Opositoal: Espectaores Mujer Negra”. Carrete a Real: Carrera, Clase y Sexo en las películas Nueva York: Routledge.
—Stiegler, Bernard (1995/2002). “La imagen discreta”. J. Derrida y B. Stiegler, Echographies of Television: Filmed Interviews (pp. 147-163). Cambridge: Polity Press.

CALEB STEIN
Down by the Hudson

website
Instagram

Published by: Palo Gallery Press
Text by: Matteo Cremonesi

Down by the Hudson [2013-2025] is published by Palo Gallery Press, with text contributions by Amitava Kumar, Anita N. Bateman, Matt Carey-Williams, and an interview with Daniel Wolff. A solo exhibition of Down by the Hudson opens at Palo Gallery, NY, at 21 E. 3rd Street, on September 10th from 6-8pm and will be on view until October 3rd, 2026, before traveling to solo exhibitions with Sixteen World Collection during Paris Photo, Book & Job Gallery in San Francisco (January, 2027), and Matt Carey-Williams Gallery in London (March 3-April 2nd, 2027). 


Down by the Hudson takes shape around a small creek on the outskirts of Poughkeepsie, New York, a city where the artist lived intermittently between 2013 and 2025. Tucked away behind a drive-in movie theater, this improvised swimming spot constitutes the geographical and affective center of a body of work that, over the years, has gradually transformed a personal experience into a broader reflection on forms of community, belonging, and representation. The creek initially appears as a marginal, almost insignificant landscape, yet it is precisely this peripheral condition that allows it to become a site of condensation: a place where bodies, desires, social differences, and conflicting imaginaries converge, giving shape to a contemporary Eden that is as idyllic as it is precarious.

The work cannot, however, be separated from the recent history of Poughkeepsie and the transformations that have reshaped the city’s social fabric. The gradual decline of industry in the area, particularly following the downsizing of IBM’s local headquarters in the 1990s, left behind an economic and human geography marked by job loss and social fragmentation. In 2016, during an election season characterized by an almost exact balance between opposing political allegiances, these tensions suddenly became visible. Like many other small American cities, Poughkeepsie revealed itself not only as a specific place, but as a local surface onto which the broader contradictions of the country were projected: industrial decline, political polarization, the erosion of traditional forms of belonging, and the growing difficulty of imagining a shared and communal space.

It is within this fracture that *Down by the Hudson* finds its position. The project does not seek to directly represent conflict or construct a documentary narrative of crisis. Instead, it shifts its gaze toward an apparently peripheral place, where the political dimension is not illustrated but persists as a subterranean pressure. The small swimming hole frequented by the artist thus becomes a space in which people from different backgrounds and circumstances meet and temporarily share a form of proximity. Its very existence is marked by a slight condition of clandestinity: local regulations prohibit gatherings, so the simple act of meeting, swimming, or spending time together takes on the character of a minor transgression. Nothing heroic, of course, but it is precisely at this reduced scale that a concrete political possibility emerges: that of temporarily reclaiming a place from its regulated functions and returning it to common use.

Photography enters this space without claiming to establish a neutral distance. The images are the result of relationships built over time, repeated encounters, and a gradual familiarity with the people portrayed. This shifts the project away from a traditional conception of the documentary, grounded in the idea of a photographer observing an external reality and rendering it through the image. Here, photography seems instead to emerge from within the relationship itself, as one of its possible consequences. The people photographed are not simply made visible; they participate in the construction of a shared situation in which play, posing, exhibition, and vulnerability become inseparable.

Andrea’s Hand with Light Rays. The Watering Hole. 2023.

Bode & Owen, Wrestling. The Watering Hole. 2022.

Boy in Black with Roots, I, The Watering Hole, 2023. 

Boy with Roots Tattoo, with Roots. The Watering Hole. 2025. 

Braily. The Watering Hole. 2020.

Hunter, with Eye-Shaped Shadow. The Watering Hole. 2025.

In a contemporary visual culture saturated with the incessant production of self-representations, it would be naïve to search within the photographic image for a condition of unmediated spontaneity. Bodies know they are being looked at, they understand the codes of photography, and they are accustomed to negotiating their presence through images that are continuously produced and shared. Down by the Hudson does not attempt to bypass this awareness in search of some presumed authenticity hidden beneath the surface. Rather, it seems to understand how posing can itself constitute a form of truth, and how intimacy does not necessarily coincide with transparency. What emerges in the photographs is instead the performative character of every encounter: a continuous movement between the desire to reveal oneself and the desire to withdraw, between the lightness of play and the exposure of vulnerability.

The relationship between photographer and subject is therefore not resolved, but kept open. It is precisely within this tension that the project finds an important part of its strength. The camera is not an invisible device that simply records what happens, but a presence around which something happens. The images do not merely document an already existing community; they participate in constructing the way this temporary community perceives itself, stages itself, and leaves a trace of its existence. A photograph, in this case, is not simply the record of a place or a moment, but the residue of a relationship.

The creek thus becomes much more than a backdrop. Nature does not appear as an uncontaminated elsewhere, separate from the city and its contradictions, nor as the romantic refuge of a community attempting to escape history. It is instead a spatial device capable of temporarily altering behavior. The water, vegetation, and isolation produce a particular condition, loosening the structures of everyday life and allowing bodies to occupy space differently. In this sense, the reference to Eden is inevitable, but this is a profoundly contemporary Eden: not an original paradise, but a precarious, marginal, and regulated space, continually threatened by its own impossibility.

The American imaginary inevitably constitutes one of the levels through which the work can be read. Summer, the river, the drive-in, young bodies, suspended time, and provincial life all point toward a deeply sedimented visual repertoire, a mythology of America constructed through cinema, photography, and popular culture. The project also belongs to a long tradition within American photography that has treated the landscape not simply as a subject to contemplate or represent, but as a territory to traverse, map, and interrogate, using it as a surface upon which the country’s economic, social, and cultural transformations might become legible. From Walker Evans and Robert Frank to William Eggleston and the period of *New Topographics*, the American landscape has often been approached as an archive of the present, a place where the forms of society become deposited and visible. Yet Down by the Hudson avoids surrendering entirely to nostalgia. The images instead seem to question the persistence of this imaginary, asking what remains of that promise of freedom when viewed from within a city marked by economic crisis and political division. The Edenic landscape does not erase the history surrounding it, just as the tenderness of these relationships does not resolve the fractures running through the community. The two dimensions remain present at once.

Matthew and Oden. The Watering Hole. 2018. 

Michael & His Friend Embracing. The Watering Hole. 2020. 

Nick, With Flower and Smoke, The Watering Hole, 2022.

Roots and Fisherman’s String. The Watering Hole. 2024. 

Statue in Water, The Watering Hole, 2020. 

TaeShawn. The Watering Hole. 2020. 

Water Mirror. The Watering Hole. 2025. 

It is perhaps precisely this coexistence that prevents the work from becoming a sentimental celebration of community. Proximity is not idealized, and encounter does not assume the value of reconciliation. What interests the artist instead is the fragile and contingent possibility that people might share a space without this necessarily translating into a common identity. The community that appears in these photographs is not a unified subject; it does not represent a fixed belonging, nor does it claim to offer an exemplary image of contemporary America. It exists only in the time of its practice: in summer, in the water, in gestures and glances, and in the possibility of returning once again to the same place.

In this sense, Down by the Hudson operates on a deliberately reduced scale, opposing the temptation of grand narratives with an insistence on what happens at the margins. Photography allows these two dimensions to be brought into relation without having to reconcile them: on the one hand, the irreducible specificity of a body, a gesture, or a glance; on the other, the collective history that continues to exert pressure on those bodies and places. The project moves precisely between these two scales, where the personal never fully coincides with the private and the political does not necessarily need to assume the explicit form of political discourse.

After years spent photographing this place and the people who inhabit it, what remains is neither the definitive portrait of a city nor the testimony of a community. What remains instead is a constellation of relationships and situations, an affective geography slowly constructed over time. The creek in Poughkeepsie becomes a figure through which to observe something broader: the need for spaces in which differences can come into contact without immediately being reduced to a function; the possibility of a proximity that does not require ideological consensus; and, above all, the persistence of forms of collective life that continue to emerge even within the most fragmented contexts.

The Eden of Down by the Hudson is therefore not a place outside history. On the contrary, it exists only within history, with all its contradictions. It is a small territory temporarily withdrawn from the established order, where freedom does not coincide with an abstract condition but with the concrete possibility of being together. Perhaps this is the work’s most political quality: not the idea of a community recovered, but the patient recording of those moments when a community, without announcing itself and without necessarily knowing that it is one, comes into being.

ALICE JANKOVIC

Green Paradox

Instagram
website

 

The Green Paradox project was born during the Swit artist residency in Gothenburg in September 2025 and developed around the figure of Scheele Green, an 18th-century pigment of extraordinary brilliance but intrinsically toxic. Discovered by chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele, who studied and worked at the ancient pharmacy Apoteket Enhörningen (the “Unicorn Pharmacy”), this color becomes the fulcrum of a visual investigation that explores the paradox between aesthetic beauty and invisible danger.

The work is configured as a chromatic archaeology in which archival images and contemporary photographs intertwine to trace a subtle line between the history of science, myth, and the transformation of matter.

The essential counterpart of this research is the city of Gothenburg, voted “Europe’s greenest city”: an urban lung where nature expresses a living and regenerating breath, placing itself in dialectical antithesis to the mineral toxicity of the historic pigment. Through an act of photographic listening, the work deconstructs the legacy of a color that still questions our present. The result is a complex chorus where chemistry meets ecology and memory becomes image, transforming the history of a color into a poetic reflection on the fragility of the balance between humanity and the environment. Scheele’s Green thus becomes the lens through which to observe nature’s capacity to persist and change, between aesthetic appeal and contemporary awareness.

Born in Genoa, Alice Jankovic is a visual artist and photographer with a solid interdisciplinary background. After completing art school, her passion for photography was ignited during a year spent in Sweden, where her encounter with Nordic light became a profound inspiration for her visual research.
After returning to Italy, she broadened her academic perspective by attending the Academy of Fine Arts in Venice (New Technologies for the Visual Arts) and, subsequently, the Academy of Genoa (Art Education). Desiring, however, to fully immerse herself in photography and specialize in a targeted manner, she interrupted her academic studies to move to Milan, where she completed a two-year intensive program at the Italian Institute of Photography (IIF). Her growing passion for publishing and photo editing led her to further explore the connection between image, text, and storytelling, attending the Photography and Literature course at the Jack London school in the Marche region and several specialized workshops in visual storytelling.
Her research focuses on the intersection of photography, installation, and editorial, evolving into a form of “visual archaeology” that integrates digital and analog photography and archival materials.
Influenced by myth and literature, the artist deconstructs the image to recontextualize it, transforming the photographic act into a tool for investigating memory. Through a constant dialogue between past and present, her works interrogate the human imprint on the landscape, hovering between documentation and evocation.

ROSIE CLEMENTS

Instagram
website

 

In her new body of work, Rosie turns the camera away from other people and toward objects, most of them consumable, and most of them hers: a vibrator, high heels, a Zoloft prescription with her legal name legible on the bottle, her husband’s cigarettes, a thong, her wedding ring, the dried bouquet she walked down the aisle with. Printed onto bubble wrap, the objects blur into something stranger: a vibrator reads as a spaceship, high heels become monolithic. It’s an intimate, anxious attempt at a self portrait, one that asks whether the objects we surround ourselves with reveal us or replace us.
Clements works in UV-printed photographs on bubble wrap, using the packaging material as a metaphor for how both goods and images are consumed and discarded. Her practice examines desire and ephemerality within digital culture, where social feeds and consumer cycles have reshaped how we relate to beauty and identity.

“When I make a photograph I’m trying to keep something,” she says, “But the image is always just the idea of what was in front of me. When I push it onto plastic through UV printing, it dissolves even further. What remains is closer to a trace than a record, a memory of a form rather than the form itself.”

Rosie Clements (*1990), is Based in Los Angeles, CA. She received her MFA in studio art from the University of Texas at Austin in 2024. Editorial clients include NYT Opinion, and her work has been featured in publications such as BOOOOOOOM, Southwest Contemporary, Dazed, and It’s Nice That. She has exhibited her work across the U.S. and internationally. Surface Tension, a two-person exhibition featuring Clements and painter Peter McRury, is on view now through July 26 at McLennon Pen Co in Austin, TX.

MICHAEL NORTHRUP

Instagram
website

 

I love irony… not exclusively, but I have a special appreciation for it.  And it underlies a lot of my work. I must have been especially influenced by my mother who would laugh at news stories like, “Santa loses fingers while stepping off helicopter to wave at kids”.  During the 50’s my older brother told me all the science fiction and horror movies we were seeing were documentaries. And my dad, being a doctor, surgeon, and coroner, would bring humor to the dinner table on things like bowel obstructions and suicides. My whole family was great at extracting humor out of tragedy and that has given me a way of seeing life.  For me creating images is all about my daily life, those meaningful pictures I’m able to extract from it, and the personal photographic vision I bring to those visual narratives.

Michael Northrup was born in 1948, grew up in Marietta Ohio, and graduated high school in 1966. Finding his course in life was a difficult path transferring 4 times before settling at Ohio University to finish his BFA in photography 1970. He spent the next 4 years traveling and building a portfolio that would get him into Grad School. In 1978 he entered the Graduate Photo Program at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago and received his MFA 1980. He married 1977, had a child 1981, and taught off and on over the next 10 years. He then moved to Baltimore to enter the commercial photo field 1990 and has been there ever since. He has 6 photo books out and continues to create photographs.

回 (huí) translates as “circle,” “time,” “to go back,” “to turn around,” and/or “to respond,” and 家 (jiā) as “home” and/or “family.” Together, they mean homecoming, and this return represents an autobiographical journey through my identity-search processes. This is an ongoing project (2018-) that depicts my gender transition while delving into the concept of intimacy, connecting the private and the home and understanding the body as a place to inhabit. It takes place between the different households where I have lived. Thus, each chapter opens a new door to delve into a new aspect of my identity. 回家 (huí jiā) captures the aesthetic exploration and physical changes my body goes through time. I explore the different possibilities of my image in it, by multiplying it, breaking it, shaping it… This way, the project challenges the limits of gender through the creation and development of someone who inhabits femininity through a transmasculine body, that is unmade to be made again, that goes toward its place of origin. By portraying people that surround me, I show the other side that accompany me and through which I also build my own sense of kinship. These photographs, which play with the codes of family portraiture, serve to question consanguinity by emphasizing the idea of adoption as a choice. The camera accompanies me by creating affective relationships and documenting vital changes. This concept addresses transitioning as a return to a place which is familiar to the body, circular and constructed as a home. The project functions as a visual diary of everyday experiences entangled in multiple identity transitions, where gender, racialization, and adoption intertwine, where both author and work mutually shape each other. Showing all the effects of treatments, my entire aesthetic change, and the evolution of someone who, at this moment, is also advancing in their own youth, 回家 (huí jiā) is an expansion through space and time.

Photographed across four years and four continents, The Canary and The Hammer details our reverence for gold and its role in humanity’s ruthless pursuit of progress. Through a mix of image, text and archival material, the project provides insight into the troubled history of gold and the complex ways it intersects with the global economy.
Gold is ubiquitous in modern life; the mineral is concealed at the heart of much of the technology we use and is, most fundamentally, a potent symbol of value, beauty, purity, greed and political power.
The Canary and The Hammer strives to connect these disparate stories—from the mania of the gold rush and the brutal world of modern mining to the sexual politics of the industry and gold’s dark role at the heart of high-tech industry.
Prompted by the financial crisis of 2008 and its stark reminder of the global west’s determination to accumulate wealth, Barnard sets out to question gold’s continued status as economic barometer amidst new intangible forms of technological high-finance. By addressing this topic through photography, Lisa Barnard in turn raises the question of how her chosen medium can respond to such abstract events and concepts. The result sketches a personal journey in which she ultimately tackles the complexity of material representation in these fragmented and troubling times.

In the wheel of economics, which transforms raw materials into manufactured goods and then into abstract entities like financial assets, gold continues to play an essential role. The king of metals, which investors always return to, a symbol of wealth but also of purity, beauty and power, gold has accompanied humanity since its origins, as a currency, as jewellery, as a standard of value, or as one of the essential materials in electronic devices.
In The Canary and The Hammer, British artist Lisa Barnard connects these multiple narratives, in which the gold rush and the brutality of mining intersect with the shadowy realms of high finance, through a variety of media that combine text, image and archival materials. The result is a work of visual research that explores photography’s capacity to express abstractions and connect them with something as tangible and earthy as a mineral.

The Oriental Scene investigates the concept of Chinoiserie architecture in the UK in the context of de-colonialism. The project uses a replica of the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing in Kew Gardens as the main object of investigation, which includes objects, drawings and documents to show how the pagoda was represented in various mediums. In the 17th and 18th centuries, while Europe was experiencing a wave of Chinoiserie, Sir William Chambers built a replica of the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing at Kew in 1762, which was destroyed by the Taiping army in 1856. No photographs of the Porcelain Tower were left before photography was widely used. There are subtle differences in the depiction of the Porcelain Tower in the imagery preserved in the East and West, leading to misunderstandings; for example, the number of storeys of the Porcelain Tower is shown in European prints and book illustrations in both nine- and ten-storey versions. However, according to Chinese Han Buddhist tradition, in most cases, the pagoda must have an odd number of storeys, and the Nanking Tower is nine. The fact that Kew’s Pagoda has ten storeys raises the suspicion that it has been misrepresented by the image, showing a slightly paradoxical relationship between reality and fiction. Prompted by the ‘wrong number of stories,’ this project explores the appropriation, de- contextualization, and reassignment of meaning to oriental symbols across time and space. The project is concerned with the interrogation of Orientalism and the authoring of visual narratives. Rethinking how pagodas have been used to create images of the East and used by the West to portray cultural otherness. It also revolves around the juxtaposition and combination of historical and contemporary artistic works and visual documents, pointing to the process of visual cultural transference regarding the pagoda. This project uses photography to present these images in a contemporary form. Through the erasure of Orientalism, the architectural redaction engages with the debate on the cultural ownership of the East, revealing the history of cultural colonisation behind the oriental scenes created by the West and the institutional problems of the museum.

Yuxing Chen (b. 1998, China) is a London- and Shanghai-based artist whose work critically engages with the historical and contemporary implications of Chinoiserie. Through photography, she examines how Orientalism has been adopted, romanticized, and perpetuated in the Western imagination. Her practice interrogates issues of decolonization, cultural difference, and the exoticized gaze, challenging dominant narratives and representations. Yuxing has been awarded the IPE Award from the Royal Photographic Society and is the winner of the Constructed Photography Global Sino Award 2024. Her works have been selected as TOP20 Chinese Contemporary Photography, finalised for the Encontros da Imagem Discovery Award(2024, PT), the Grand Prix Images Vevey (2023, Switzerland), long-listed for the OD Photo Prize (2023, UK), selected for the Copenhagen Photo Festival(2024, DK), Athens Photo Festival (2024, GK ), the PhMuseum Days Exhibition(2023, Italy), nominated for the 4th 1839 Photography Prize(2022, China). Her work has been exhibited widely in Italy, England, Germany and other countries. Her work is in private and public collections at the Zhejiang Art Museum and the University of the Arts London. She has been featured in the British Journal of Photography, Chinese Photography, RPS Journal, GUP magazine and many other press.

Resetting the school system is one of the unfinished tasks of our time and perhaps one of the most complicated. Karolina Wojtas’s Abzgram project (a nonsense word invented by the artist, which, when the letters are rearranged, becomes bazgram, meaning to doodle or to draw aimlessly in Polish) takes as its starting point the rigidity of the Polish education system and the artist’s own childhood experiences. She recalls being “confined” by countless, almost military rules of conduct that limited the development of her creativity and imposed a very narrow idea of ​​what could be considered art. With its saturated colours and delirious compositions, Abzgram responds to this iron discipline with a visual act of revenge, imagining what a different sort of school would be like. A school that fosters imagination, fun, humour, and the development of expressive abilities, that sees learning as a process of personal experimentation and that even questions whether education is truly necessary or if other ways of acquiring and applying knowledge can be invented.

Born in Poland in 1996, Karolina Wojtas graduated from the Lodz Film School and the Institute of Creative Photography in the Czech Republic. In the summer of 2019, she opened her own museum in her hometown in Poland. Wojtas has exhibited her work in numerous solo and group exhibitions in Poland and internationally in Foam Amsterdam (2021), Noorderlicht International Photography Festival (2020), Naga Gallery in Warsaw (2020) or Bratislava Photography Month (2019). Awards and recognitions for her work include a nomination for the EMoP Arendt 2023 award, reGeneration 4: The Challenges of Photography and its Museum for Tomorrow at the Musée de l’Elysée, a special mention at Plat(f)orm 2020 at the Fotomuseum Winterthur, the C/O Berlin Award (2022), the ING Unseen Talent Award (2019) in Amsterdam, and the Tiff Open (2018) at the Tiff Festival Wrocław. Her work has been featured in The Guardian, Internazionale, The British Journal of Photography, Lampoon Magazine, L’uomo Vogue, Superpaper, Tampon – Ordinary Magazine, Causette, and Das Magazin Switzerland.

Getxophoto is an image festival created and managed by Begihandi, that has been taking place in Getxo—Basque Country, Euskadi—since 2007. This festival is part of a cultural ecosystem with the aim of being more participatory, hybrid, committed and sustainable. This thematic Festival is conceived as a platform that addresses contemporary challenges through different proposals, from visual storytellers around the world, in an attempt to create spaces for reflection and establish a collective conversation. Getxophoto is characterized by the radical defense of public space (both physical and online). For this reason, most of its programme is composed of outdoor installations, highlighting, on the one hand, the link between the image and the environment and, on the other, generating a more horizontal and participatory relationship with the public.

This year, after PAUSE, PLAY and REC, the festival reaches a milestone: its 20th edition. The common thread for this anniversary edition could only be… RESET—a button that invites us to reboot the system. Anniversaries are moments to celebrate and rejoice, but also excellent opportunities to look back and take stock, to review our archives and get a glimpse of what we have changed; and equally a time to project forward with renewed energy, just as when soil is ploughed so that seeds can be sown again. The edition therefore welcomes proposals that address experiences of change, reworking, recycling and reinvention; of life cycles and celebrations; of individual or collective stories of resetting—a system reboot in any of its many forms.
